query_preview:
..Today...Moisture from Hurricane Rachel has moved 
into much of northern Arizona this morning, with PWAT values near 
or exceeding daily record levels. Several areas of showers and 
thunderstorms, with embedded heavy rainfall, are moving across 
northern Arizona this morning. The heaviest of which is to the 
west over Mohave County. As the vort max from Rachel moves 
northeastward into Utah, the upper-level jet over Arizona begins 
to increase. This should lead to a further increase in coverage of
showers and thunderstorms into the afternoon hours, before 
gradually diminishing later this evening. Gusty southerly winds 
are also expected today, with gusts upwards of 45 to 55 mph 
expected. Some locally higher gusts will be possible downwind of 
the higher terrain.

Latest HREF and REFS guidance highlight the greatest potential for 
heavy rainfall to be through this afternoon, and mainly from western 
Coconino county, down to Gila and Yavapai counties. However, with 
storm motions of 50-60 mph, the overall residency time of any one 
storm has been limited so far today. Thus, the greatest flash flood 
threat will exist in any rain sensitive locations (burn scars, slot 
canyons, and urban areas) and where storms tend to train over one 
area for an extended period of time. A Flash Flood Watch remains in 
effect until 5 AM MST Monday to cover this threat.

Given the high shear environment, 40-60 kts in the 0-6 km layer, an 
isolated strong to severe thunderstorm is not out of the question. 
The limiting factor to this will be the lack of day time heating, 
thereby limiting the instability going into this afternoon. The main 
threat with any storm will be damaging winds, however an brief 
isolated tornado can no be totally ruled out. The greatest risk area 
looks to mainly be across northern Gila and Yavapai counties through 
the early afternoon hours.

Monday and Tuesday...As the remnants of Rachel lift to the north, a 
strong upper-level low dives southward into the Great Basin. An 
enhanced upper-level jet over Arizona will keep showers and 
thunderstorms in the forecast each day. However, model soundings 
show a much more shallow moisture profile as drier air moves in 
aloft. Thus, the greatest likelihood for precipitation will be in 
the higher terrain where orographic effects will aid in vertical 
motion. Given the more shallow moisture profile, the flash flood 
threat look to be lesser and more localized.

Winds look to remain gusty given the jet in place, however, not 
nearly as strong as today. The highest gusts will mainly be found 
immediately downwind of the Mogollon Rim into the Little Colorado 
River Valley, where gusts of 40-50 mph will be possible. Given the 
more limited coverage of the stronger winds, a Wind Advisory does 
not appear necessary at this time. Cooler conditions look to set in 
for the start of the work week as well.

Wednesday through Saturday...By the middle of the week, the trough 
begins to lift out of Arizona and into the northern Plains. 
Remnant moisture will leave the potential for a few isolated 
showers Arizona the higher terrain of eastern Arizona, but dry 
conditions are otherwise expected for the day. Lighter winds and 
slightly warmer conditions are also expected.

Guidance seems to have come into a bit more agreement with the low 
breaking off from the jet, and briefly becoming a closed-low over 
the southwest. Therefore, temperatures look to warm a few degrees 
but remain cooler than normal. Gusty northeast winds look to set in 
for Thursday and Friday, with the strong pressure gradient in place 
with a surface low to the southwest and surface high pressure over 
Colorado.

Drier air will keep dry conditions in the forecast for Thursday. 
However, as the upper-level low begins to retrograde over Arizona, 
some moisture does look to work it's way back into eastern Arizona 
on Friday and spreading westward into Saturday. Of the ensemble 
guidance, the EPS members tend to favor a better chances for 
showers, given that they have maintained a stronger low, while the 
GEFS members favor the drier solution with the low being weaker and 
further south. Therefore, uncertainty does still remain in the exact 
details of the extended forecast period.
